analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies buy drugs at discounted federal prices and sell them cheaper to Medicare seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in House committees when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let any pharmacy sign an agreement to sell prescription drugs to Medicare beneficiaries at the discounted prices the federal government already pays through the Federal Supply Schedule, plus a small administrative fee. Pharmacies could buy as much as they sell to seniors, and hospice programs could use the same arrangement. The stated goal was to end the gap in which seniors paid far more for the same drugs than big insurers and hospitals pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially the many without prescription drug coverage, who would pay closer to the lowest federal price for their drugs. Pharmacies that choose to participate would gain a purchasing channel that could help them compete for senior customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare without drug coverage

how_it_helps.text: Participating pharmacies could buy covered outpatient drugs at the Federal Supply Schedule price — the discounted price already available to federal agencies — plus a small administrative fee [S3].

The bill's findings state that seniors pay over twice what manufacturers charge favored customers like HMOs and hospital chains, and that lower drug prices would also lower Medicare costs to taxpayers [S3].
Hospice programs could arrange to deliver drugs to terminally ill beneficiaries at the reduced price [S3].
The bill claims no cost to taxpayers, since it uses the existing federal discount and existing drug distribution methods [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, which would lose the premium prices seniors currently pay when the cheapest federal price is extended to a nationwide network of pharmacies serving Medicare beneficiaries.

drawbacks.text: Participation is voluntary on both sides: pharmacies must opt in, and the bill relies on Federal Supply Schedule prices that manufacturers negotiate with the government, so savings depend on how deep those discounts are and how many pharmacies join [S3].

The bill does not cap prices or mandate coverage; it channels the discount only to Medicare beneficiaries through participating pharmacies, so non-beneficiaries still pay whatever the market charges [S2].
The administrative fee added on top of the federal price, and the Secretary's discretion in determining it, could reduce the savings seniors actually see [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors paying the highest prices in the market for essential drugs, the benefits are large and the taxpayer cost is claimed to be zero, since it piggybacks on discounts the government already gets. The main honest objection is design: it is a voluntary purchasing channel rather than a mandate or price cap, so its reach depends entirely on how many pharmacies join and how deep the federal discount runs. Still, the burden falls on drug makers' pricing power, not on patients or taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 1998, referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bud Cramer (D-AL) introduced the bill on October 10, 1998, less than a month before the 105th Congress's elections and final weeks [S1].

It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and on October 21, 1998, to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment — the last action ever taken [S5].
It attracted no cosponsors in its three months of existence [S4].
Neither committee ever reported the bill, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept their pricing structure, since seniors continued paying retail prices well above what HMOs and federal agencies pay. Nothing changed for seniors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers kept charging seniors full price

for.name: Rep. Robert E. (Bud) Cramer Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend Federal Supply Schedule drug prices to Medicare beneficiaries through participating pharmacies.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee on October 21, 1998, and never held a markup or reported it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for Medicare-related provisions and never acted on the bill.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation extending government-negotiated discount prices to seniors, an issue the bill's own findings address.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had only one sponsor, a Democrat, with no cosponsors, so the partisan shape cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill targets their practice of charging seniors over twice what favored customers like HMOs pay, by extending the lowest federal price to a pharmacy network serving Medicare beneficiaries. Their pricing power over the biggest consumer group of prescription drugs was what the bill would have curtailed.

Participating pharmacies would gain access to the Federal Supply Schedule price on drugs sold to Medicare beneficiaries, a purchasing advantage they currently lack. Their gain runs alongside seniors' savings.

industries.industry: Medicare Advantage plans and hospice programs
industries.note: Hospice programs could procure discounted drugs for terminally ill beneficiaries; HMOs and other favored customers already pay low prices and would face no direct change.
